title: Salt in the water
hookLine: a proud young graduate comes home, and his father hands him a glass of salt water
carry: tat tvam asi: like salt in water, you are that

cards: A young man named Shvetaketu comes home after twelve years of study. He's twenty-four, he's memorized the sacred texts, and he is, the Upanishad says, conceited, thinking himself very learned. You know this person.
Maybe you've been this person, home from your first year of college. His father, Uddalaka, asks one quiet question.
Did you ask for the teaching by which what hasn't been heard becomes heard, and what hasn't been understood becomes understood? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means.
So his father starts teaching, with things from the kitchen.

teach.b: This is the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, one of the oldest and most important Upanishads. The father gives lesson after lesson, and one of the most well-known uses salt.
Put this salt in water, he says, and come back in the morning. The son does. Now bring me the salt.
Shvetaketu can't find it; it's dissolved. Taste the water from the top, says the father.

teach.h: SALTY AT THE TOP, MIDDLE, BOTTOM.

teach.b: From the bottom? Salty. The salt is everywhere in the water, and you can't see it anywhere.
Then the father says the line this road is built on.

teach.h: THE SUBTLE ESSENCE IS THE SELF.
teach.b: That subtle essence is in everything; it is the real; it is the Self. And then three Sanskrit words: tat tvam asi. You are that, Shvetaketu.
He says it nine times in the chapter. What does it mean?

Here the great schools you met a few weeks ago part ways, and none is ranked. Shankara's Advaita hears plain identity: your deepest self and the ultimate reality are one, like the salt and the water's taste.
Ramanuja hears it as the way a body belongs to its life: you exist in that, and for that.

Madhva's school reads the same words differently again, and keeps the soul distinct. All three are Hindu readings of the same kitchen lesson. The jnana road is the road of seeing this, not just repeating it.
Shvetaketu knew a lot of words. His father wanted him to taste the water.

how: Tat tvam asi from the Chandogya Upanishad is counted among the four mahavakyas, the great sayings of the Upanishads, and is studied and meditated on across Vedanta traditions, each reading it in its own way.

o: a name for a sacred river
action, even the act of looking closely
the opposite of knowledge and study

games.q: the salt lesson — tap the pairs.
p: the proud son, home after twelve years
the father who teaches with salt

s: Shvetaketu found the salt in the morning
it had dissolved. he couldn't see it, but the water was salty at the top, middle and bottom.
the father says 'tat tvam asi' more than once
the refrain comes nine times in the sixth chapter of the Chandogya.
every Hindu school reads 'you are that' the same way
Advaita, Ramanuja's school and Madhva's school read it differently.

games.q: you're Uddalaka. your son is proud of how much he's memorized, but he's missed the point. how do you teach him?
o: give him another book to memorize.
put salt in water and ask him to find it.
tell him he's not ready and send him away.
games.why: the father teaches with the kitchen: salt he can't see, but can taste everywhere. then: tat tvam asi, you are that.

practice: Imagine a glass of water with salt dissolved in it: you can't see the salt, but taste it anywhere and there it is.
Turn that picture gently toward yourself: is something present in every part of your day, your moods, your memories, the quiet between thoughts, without ever being seen?
Don't try to name it; just notice the taste of being here, top, middle and bottom, and if you pray, rest in that as a prayer.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and on the jnana road the action is looking: Shvetaketu tasting the water until he sees.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tat, that + tvam, you + asi, are. Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 and the refrain after it.

carryVoice: Take this with you: tat tvam asi. Like salt in water, unseen and everywhere: you are that. That's day three hundred four.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1 (Shvetaketu returns at twenty-four) and 6.13 (salt in water)
